name: Kang-Petrov Arms KP-19FL 'Flatline'
description:
The KP-19FL is a suppressor-optimized variant of the KP-19, featuring a threaded and ported barrel, a raised sight system that clears suppressor bodies, and a heavier recoil spring assembly calibrated to cycle reliably with the back-pressure generated by can-equipped operation. It chambers 9x19mm Standard exclusively—9x19mm Caseless is incompatible with most suppressor designs due to the different combustion signature. The slide is lightened at the rear to maintain cycling speed, and the ejection port is widened and polished to prevent the case tumbling that suppressor-induced pressure changes can cause in stock designs. The factory finish is non-reflective matte black, and the front sight is tritium-inlaid as standard.

The KP-19FL is not a gun Kang-Petrov sells loudly. It appears in their catalog under 'specialized applications' and the product page is three lines of text without images. Everyone who needs one knows it exists. The legal framework around suppressor ownership in GLMZ is technically permissive—suppressors require a secondary registration form and a 90-day processing window—but Arcturus Civil Security treats suppressor-equipped firearms with consistent suspicion regardless of paperwork. The Flatline sells to people who accept that tradeoff: security consultants, industrial noise-abatement operators (a category that exists entirely to provide legal cover), and people who prefer not to announce their location when the situation goes wrong.

Used suppressed, the KP-19FL produces a report that sounds, from a distance of 30 meters, like a heavy staple gun or a small pneumatic tool—the kind of sound that industrial zones generate constantly and that no one investigates. That's not an accident of engineering. The raised night sights glow faintly green in the dark, and operators who run the Flatline seriously almost always have a weapon light on the rail as well, since the situations where you want quiet are frequently also the situations where it's dark.
specifications:
caliber: 9x19mm Standard
effective_range: 50m
rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic
magazine_capacity: 17 rounds
weight: 0.81 kg (without suppressor)
tactical_use: The KP-19FL is optimized for operations where noise discipline is a primary concern. Operators almost always run it with a suppressor, accepting the added length in exchange for a significant reduction in acoustic and muzzle-flash signature. The raised sights and widened ejection port address the two most common suppressor-related malfunctions. Without a can, it functions identically to a standard KP-19 but with slightly increased muzzle velocity from the ported barrel. The restricted license requirement means operators who carry one have accepted a level of scrutiny that filters for professionalism.
cultural_context: In GLMZ, a suppressor-configured pistol occupies a specific social position: legal enough to own, suspicious enough to draw attention. Carrying a Flatline to a routine job is the kind of thing that gets noted. In the fixer community, it's considered a sign that someone has thought carefully about their work—for better or worse. Corp security officers who encounter one tend to call for backup.
story_hooks: A Flatline registered to a Slagworks 'noise abatement' contractor was used in the killing of a union organizer—the suppressor registration is current, the paperwork is perfect, but the contractor doesn't exist as a legal entity before eight months ago.

Kyle Corbin-Vasik is offered a KP-19FL as payment for a job. The gun is clean, properly licensed, and clearly expensive—which raises the question of why the client is paying in firearms instead of Quanta.
